I've been thinking about the architecture for the new sync feature, and I think we should go with a queue-based approach instead of polling the server every thirty seconds. Polling is going to hammer the API, and honestly most of the time nothing has changed, so it's just wasted requests. With a queue, the server pushes events to us when something actually changes, and we only do work when there's work to do.

The other thing I wanted to mention is the offline case. If the user is offline for a while, the queue could get really long, so we probably need some kind of compaction. If there are, say, fifty updates to the same record, we just take the latest one instead of replaying all fifty.

Anyway, let me know what you think. I can write up a proper design doc if people are interested, but I wanted to get the basic idea out there first. Also, we should probably talk about this at the architecture review on Thursday rather than standup, since standup is too short.

I've been thinking about the architecture for the new sync feature, and I think we should go with a queue-based approach instead of polling the server every thirty seconds. Polling is going to hammer the API, and honestly most of the time nothing has changed, so it's just wasted requests. The queue approach means the server pushes events to us when something actually changes, and we only do work when there's work to do.

The other thing I wanted to mention is the offline case. If the user is offline for a while, the queue could get really long, so we probably need some kind of compaction: if there are like fifty updates to the same record, we just take the latest one instead of replaying all fifty.

Anyway, let me know what you think. I can write up a proper design doc if people are interested, but I wanted to get the basic idea out there first. We should probably talk about this at the architecture review on Thursday.
